[[File:Marsh Butte and Geikie Peak, Grand Canyon.jpg|right|thumb|upright=1.35|The [[Grand Canyon]], an incision through layers of sedimentary rocks.]]
{{Geology sidebar}}

In [[geology]], a '''rock''' (also called a '''stone''') is any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of [[mineral]]s or [[mineraloid]] matter. It is categorized by the minerals included, its [[Chemical compound|chemical composition]], and the way in which it is formed. Rocks form the Earth's outer solid layer, the [[Earth's crust|crust]], and most of its interior, except for the liquid [[Earth's outer core|outer core]] and pockets of [[magma]] in the [[asthenosphere]]. The study of rocks involves multiple subdisciplines of geology, including [[petrology]] and [[mineralogy]]. It may be limited to rocks found on Earth, or it may include [[planetary geology]] that studies the rocks of other celestial objects.

Rocks are usually grouped into three main groups: [[igneous rock]]s, [[sedimentary rock]]s and [[metamorphic rock]]s. Igneous rocks are formed when [[magma]] cools in the Earth's crust, or [[lava]] cools on the ground surface or the seabed. Sedimentary rocks are formed by [[diagenesis]] and [[lithification]] of [[sediment]]s, which in turn are formed by the [[weathering]], transport, and [[Deposition (geology)|deposition]] of existing rocks. Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing rocks are subjected to such high pressures and temperatures that they are transformed without significant melting.

Humanity has made use of rocks since the time the earliest humans lived. This early period, called the [[Stone Age]], saw the development of many stone tools. Stone was then used as a major component in the construction of buildings and early [[infrastructure]]. [[Mining]] developed to extract rocks from the Earth and obtain the minerals within them, including [[metal]]s. Modern technology has allowed the development of new human-made rocks and rock-like substances, such as [[concrete]].

== Study ==
{{Further|Geology|Petrology|Mineralogy}}
Geology is the study of Earth and its components, including the study of rock formations. Petrology is the study of the character and origin of rocks. Mineralogy is the study of the mineral components that create rocks. The study of rocks and their components has contributed to the geological understanding of Earth's history, the [[archaeological]] understanding of human history, and the development of [[engineering]] and [[technology]] in human society.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Haldar |first=S. K. |title=Introduction to Mineralogy and Petrology |publisher=Elsevier Science |year=2013 |isbn=9780124167100 |pages=1–37 |chapter=Introduction}}</ref>

While the [[history of geology]] includes many theories of rocks and their origins that have persisted throughout human history, the study of rocks was developed as a formal science during the 19th century. [[Plutonism]] was developed as a theory during this time, and the discovery of [[radioactive decay]] in 1896 allowed for the [[radiometric dating]] of rocks. Understanding of [[plate tectonics]] developed in the second half of the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=O'Hara |first=Kieran D. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/brief-history-of-geology/7F17585841AA085A55B5028503EA7742 |title=A Brief History of Geology |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-316-80999-0 |edition=1 |pages=247–259 |chapter=The Structure of Geological Revolutions |doi=10.1017/9781316809990.013 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/brief-history-of-geology/structure-of-geological-revolutions/D6579716D9A1E3D5795A6DD27C443D53}}</ref>

==Classification==
{{See also|Formation of rocks}}
[[File:Kummakivi balancing rock in Ruokolahti, Finland.jpg|left|thumb|A [[balancing rock]] called ''[[Kummakivi]]'' (literally ''"strange stone"'')<ref>[https://unusualplaces.org/kummakivi/ Kummakivi], Unusual Places.org.</ref>]]

Rocks are composed primarily of grains of minerals, which are [[crystalline solids]] formed from atoms [[chemical bond|chemically bonded]] into an orderly structure.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nesse |first1=William D. |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontomi0000ness_m9a6 |title=Introduction to mineralogy |date=2000 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780195106916 |location=New York |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|3}} Some rocks also contain [[mineraloid]]s, which are rigid, mineral-like substances, such as [[volcanic glass]],<ref name=Blatt>{{cite book |last1=Blatt |first1=Harvey |first2=Robert J. |last2=Tracy |date=1996 |title=Petrology |publisher=W.H. Freeman |edition=2nd |isbn=978-0-7167-2438-4}}</ref>{{rp|55,79}}that lack crystalline structure. The types and abundance of minerals in a rock are determined by the manner in which it was formed.

Most rocks contain [[silicate minerals]], compounds that include silica tetrahedra in their [[crystal lattice]], and account for about one-third of all known mineral species and about 95% of the [[Crust (geology)|earth's crust]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Heinen |first1=Wouter |last2=Oehler |first2=John H. |editor1-last=Trudinger |editor1-first=P.A. |editor2-last=Swaine |editor2-first=D.J. |title=Biogeochemical Cycling of Mineral-Forming Elements |date=1979 |publisher=Elsevier |location=Amsterdam |isbn=9780080874623 |page=431 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uqm3-V7Xr-cC&pg=PA431 |access-date=13 April 2020 |chapter=Evolutionary Aspects of Biological Involvement in the Cycling of Silica}}</ref> The proportion of [[silica]] in rocks and minerals is a major factor in determining their names and properties.<ref name="Wilson1995"/>

[[File:DirkvdM rocks.jpg|right|thumb|Rock [[outcrop]] along a mountain creek near [[Orosí]], [[Costa Rica]].]]
Rocks are classified according to characteristics such as mineral and chemical composition, [[permeability (earth sciences)|permeability]], [[Texture (geology)|texture]] of the constituent particles, and [[Particle size (grain size)|particle size]]. These physical properties are the result of the processes that formed the rocks.<ref name=Blatt/> Over the course of time, rocks can be transformed from one type into another, as described by a geological model called the [[rock cycle]]. This transformation produces three general classes of rock: [[igneous rock|igneous]], [[sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] and [[metamorphic rock|metamorphic]].

These three classes are subdivided into many groups. There are, however, no hard-and-fast boundaries between allied rocks. By increase or decrease in the proportions of their minerals, they pass through gradations from one to the other; the distinctive structures of one kind of rock may thus be traced, gradually merging into those of another. Hence the definitions adopted in rock names simply correspond to selected points in a continuously graduated series.<ref name=EB1911>{{EB1911|wstitle=Petrology |volume=21 |page=327 |inline=1 |first=John Smith |last=Flett |author-link=John Flett (geologist)}}</ref>

===Igneous rock===
{{Main|Igneous rock}}
[[File:GabbroRockCreek1.jpg|thumb|Sample of igneous [[gabbro]]]]
Igneous rock (derived from the [[Latin]] word ''igneus'', meaning ''of fire'', from ''ignis'' meaning ''fire'')<ref>{{cite web |title="igneous, adj." |work=OED Online |date=March 2021 |publisher=Oxford University Press |url=https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/91193?redirectedFrom=igneous |access-date=17 April 2021}}</ref> is formed through the cooling and [[freezing|solidification]] of [[magma]] or [[lava]]. This magma may be derived from partial melts of pre-existing rocks in either a [[planet]]'s [[mantle (geology)|mantle]] or [[crust (geology)|crust]]. Typically, the melting of rocks is caused by one or more of three processes: an increase in temperature, a decrease in pressure, or a change in composition.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Philpotts |first1=Anthony R. |last2=Ague |first2=Jay J. |title=Principles of igneous and metamorphic petrology |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |isbn=9780521880060 |edition=2nd}}</ref>{{rp|591–599}}

Igneous rocks are divided into two main categories:
* [[Plutonic]] or [[Intrusion|intrusive]] rocks result when magma cools and [[crystallization|crystallizes]] slowly within the [[Earth's crust]]. A common example of this type is [[granite]].
* Volcanic or [[extrusive (geology)|extrusive]] rocks result from magma reaching the surface either as lava or ''fragmental ejecta'', forming minerals such as [[pumice]] or [[basalt]].<ref name=Blatt/>

Magmas tend to become richer in silica as they rise towards the Earth's surface, a process called ''[[magma differentiation]]''. This occurs both because minerals low in silica crystallize out of the magma as it begins to cool ([[Bowen's reaction series]]) and because the magma assimilates some of the crustal rock through which it ascends (''[[country rock (geology)|country rock]]''), and crustal rock tends to be high in silica. Silica content is thus the most important chemical criterion for classifying igneous rock.<ref name="Wilson1995"/> The content of [[alkali metal oxide]]s is next in importance.<ref>{{cite book |editor-first1=R. W. |editor-last1=Le Maitre |editor-first2=A. |editor-last2=Streckeisen |editor-first3=B. |editor-last3=Zanettin |editor-first4=M. J. |editor-last4=Le Bas |editor-first5=B. |editor-last5=Bonin |editor-first6=P. |editor-last6=Bateman |editor-first7=G. |editor-last7=Bellieni |editor-first8=A. |editor-last8=Dudek |editor-first9=S. |editor-last9=Efremova |editor-first10=J. |editor-last10=Keller |editor-first11=J. |editor-last11=Lamere |editor-first12=P. A. |editor-last12=Sabine |editor-first13=R. |editor-last13=Schmid |editor-first14=H. |editor-last14=Sorensen |editor-first15=A. R. |editor-last15=Woolley |title=Igneous Rocks: A Classification and Glossary of Terms, Recommendations of the International Union of Geological Sciences, Subcommission of the Systematics of Igneous Rocks |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2002 |edition=2nd |isbn=0-521-66215-X}}</ref>

About 65% of the Earth's crust by volume consists of igneous rocks. Of these, 66% are basalt and [[gabbro]], 16% are granite, and 17% [[granodiorite]] and [[diorite]]. Only 0.6% are [[syenite]] and 0.3% are [[ultramafic]]. The [[oceanic crust]] is 99% basalt, which is an igneous rock of [[mafic]] composition. Granite and similar rocks, known as [[granitoids]], dominate the [[continental crust]].<ref name="condie">{{cite book |last1=Condie |first1=Kent C. |author-link1=Kent Condie |title=Plate Tectonics & Crustal Evolution |date=2015 |publisher=Pergamon |location=New York|edition=2nd |isbn=9781483100142 |page=68 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lO7fBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA68 |access-date=13 April 2020}}</ref><ref name="BucherGrapes2011"/>

===Sedimentary rock===
{{Main|Sedimentary rock}}
[[File:"Liesegang banding" in quartzose sandstone (Upper Paleozoic; quarry near Crossville, Tennessee, USA) 2 (40280403530).jpg|thumb|Sedimentary [[sandstone]] with [[iron oxide]] bands]]
Sedimentary rocks are formed at the earth's surface by the accumulation and cementation of fragments of earlier rocks, minerals, and organisms<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/principlesofgeol00gill|url-access=registration|title=Principles of Geology|last=Gilluly|first=James|date=1959|publisher=W.H. Freeman|author-link=James Gilluly|df=dmy-all}}</ref> or as chemical precipitates and organic growths in water ([[sedimentation]]). This process causes [[clastic]] [[sediment]]s (pieces of rock) or [[organic matter|organic]] particles ([[detritus]]) to settle and accumulate or for minerals to chemically [[precipitation (chemistry)|precipitate]] ([[evaporite]]) from a [[Solution (chemistry)|solution]]. The particulate matter then undergoes compaction and [[cementation (geology)|cementation]] at moderate temperatures and pressures ([[diagenesis]]).<ref name=Blatt/>{{rp|265–280}}<ref name="boggs-2006">{{cite book |last1=Boggs |first1=Sam |title=Principles of sedimentology and stratigraphy |date=2006 |publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall |location=Upper Saddle River, N.J. |isbn=0131547283 |edition=4th}}</ref>{{rp|147–154}}

Before being deposited, sediments are formed by [[weathering]] of earlier rocks by [[erosion]] in a source area and then transported to the place of deposition by [[water]], [[wind]], [[ice]], [[Mass wasting|mass movement]] or [[glacier]]s (agents of [[denudation]]).<ref name=Blatt /> About 7.9% of the crust by volume is composed of sedimentary rocks, with 82% of those being shales, while the remainder consists of 6% limestone and 12% sandstone and [[arkose]]s.<ref name="BucherGrapes2011"/> Sedimentary rocks often contain [[fossil]]s. Sedimentary rocks form under the influence of gravity and typically are deposited in horizontal or near horizontal layers or [[strata]], and may be referred to as stratified rocks.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Monroe |first1=James S. |last2=Wicander |first2=Reed |title=The Changing Earth: Exploring Geology and Evolution |date=2008 |publisher=Brooks/Cole |location=Belmont, CA |isbn=9780495554806 |page=438 |edition=5th |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jFPMa4MxwJkC&pg=PA438 |access-date=13 April 2020}}</ref>

Sediment and the particles of [[Clastic rock|clastic]] sedimentary rocks can be further classified by [[grain size]]. The smallest sediments are [[clay]], followed by [[silt]], [[sand]], and [[gravel]]. Some systems include [[Cobble (geology)|cobbles]] and [[boulder]]s as measurements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blott |first1=Simon J. |last2=Pye |first2=Kenneth |date=2012 |title=Particle size scales and classification of sediment types based on particle size distributions: Review and recommended procedures |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-3091.2012.01335.x |journal=Sedimentology |language=en |volume=59 |issue=7 |pages=2071–2096 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-3091.2012.01335.x |bibcode=2012Sedim..59.2071B |s2cid=130084299 |issn=0037-0746|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Metamorphic rock===
{{Main|Metamorphic rock}}
[[File:Skagit-gneiss-Cascades.jpg|thumb|Metamorphic banded [[gneiss]]]]
Metamorphic rocks are formed by subjecting any rock type—sedimentary rock, igneous rock or another older metamorphic rock—to different [[temperature]] and [[pressure]] conditions than those in which the original rock was formed. This process is called [[metamorphism]], meaning to "change in form". The result is a profound change in physical properties and chemistry of the stone. The original rock, known as the [[protolith]], transforms into other mineral types or other forms of the same minerals, by [[Recrystallization (geology)|recrystallization]].<ref name=Blatt /> The temperatures and pressures required for this process are always higher than those found at the Earth's surface: temperatures greater than 150 to 200&nbsp;°C and pressures greater than 1500&nbsp;bars.<ref>Blatt, Harvey and Robert J. Tracy, ''Petrology'', W.H.Freeman, 2nd ed., 1996, p. 355 {{ISBN|0-7167-2438-3}}</ref> This occurs, for example, when [[continental plates]] collide.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lillie |first1=Robert J. |title=Parks and plates : the geology of our national parks, monuments, and seashores |date=2005 |publisher=W.W. Norton |isbn=0393924076 |edition=1st |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|31–33, 134–139}} Metamorphic rocks compose 27.4% of the crust by volume.<ref name="BucherGrapes2011"/>

The three major classes of metamorphic rock are based upon the formation mechanism. An intrusion of magma that heats the surrounding rock causes contact metamorphism—a temperature-dominated transformation. Pressure metamorphism occurs when sediments are buried deep under the ground; pressure is dominant, and temperature plays a smaller role. This is termed burial metamorphism, and it can result in rocks such as [[jade]]. Where both heat and pressure play a role, the mechanism is termed regional metamorphism. This is typically found in mountain-building regions.<ref name="Wilson1995"/>

Depending on the structure, metamorphic rocks are divided into two general categories. Those that possess a texture are referred to as [[Foliation (geology)|foliated]]; the remainders are termed non-foliated. The name of the rock is then determined based on the types of minerals present. [[Schist]]s are foliated rocks that are primarily composed of [[Lamella (materials)|lamellar minerals]] such as [[mica]]s. A [[gneiss]] has visible bands of differing [[lightness]], with a common example being the granite gneiss. Other varieties of foliated rock include [[slate]]s, [[phyllite]]s, and [[mylonite]]. Familiar examples of non-foliated metamorphic rocks include [[marble]], [[soapstone]], and [[Serpentine group|serpentine]]. This branch contains [[quartzite]]—a metamorphosed form of [[sandstone]]—and [[hornfels]].<ref name="Wilson1995"/>

== Extraterrestrial rocks ==
{{Main|Planetary geology}}
Though most understanding of rocks comes from those of Earth, rocks make up many of the universe's celestial bodies. In the [[Solar System]], [[Mars]], [[Venus]], and [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] are composed of rock, as are many [[natural satellite]]s, [[asteroid]]s, and [[meteoroid]]s. [[Meteorite]]s that fall to Earth provide evidence of extraterrestrial rocks and their composition. They are typically heavier than rocks on Earth. Asteroid rocks can also be brought to Earth through space missions, such as the ''[[Hayabusa]]'' mission.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kwok |first=Sun |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-32802-2 |title=Stardust: The Cosmic Seeds of Life |publisher=Springer |year=2013 |isbn=9783642328022 |pages=11–23 |chapter=Rocks and Dust in the Planetary Neighborhood |series=Astronomers' Universe |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-32802-2_2 |author-link=Sun Kwok |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-32802-2_2}}</ref> [[Moon rock|Lunar rocks]] and [[Martian rocks]] have also been studied.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Allen |first1=Carlton |last2=Allton |first2=Judith |last3=Lofgren |first3=Gary |last4=Righter |first4=Kevin |last5=Zolensky |first5=Michael |date=2011 |title=Curating NASA's extraterrestrial samples—Past, present, and future |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0009281911000031 |journal=Geochemistry |language=en |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1016/j.chemer.2010.12.003|bibcode=2011ChEG...71....1A |hdl=2060/20100042395 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Human use==
[[File:TallOvoo.JPG|thumb|left|Ceremonial [[cairn]] of rocks, an [[ovoo]], from [[Mongolia]]]]

The use of rock has had a huge impact on the cultural and technological development of the human race. Rock has been used by humans and other [[hominids]] for at least [[paleolithic|2.5&nbsp;million years]].<ref>William Haviland, Dana Walrath, Harald Prins, Bunny McBride, ''Evolution and Prehistory: The Human Challenge'', p. 166</ref> [[Lithic technology]] marks some of the oldest and continuously used technologies. The mining of rock for its metal content has been one of the most important factors of human advancement, and has progressed at different rates in different places, in part because of the kind of metals available from the rock of a region.

=== Anthropic rock ===
{{Main|Anthropic rock}}
Anthropic rock is synthetic or restructured rock formed by human activity. Concrete is recognized as a human-made rock constituted of natural and processed rock and having been developed since [[Ancient Rome]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fookes |first1=Peter G. |last2=Walker |first2=Mike J. |date=2010 |title=Concrete: a man-made rock? |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2451.2010.00748.x |journal=Geology Today |language=en |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=65–71 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2451.2010.00748.x|bibcode=2010GeolT..26...65F |s2cid=129456840 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Rock can also be modified with other substances to develop new forms, such as [[epoxy granite]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McKeown |first1=P.A. |last2=Morgan |first2=G.H. |date=1979 |title=Epoxy granite: a structural material for precision machines |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0141635979901041 |journal=Precision Engineering |language=en |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=227–229 |doi=10.1016/0141-6359(79)90104-1|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Artificial stone]] has also been developed, such as [[Coade stone]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freestone |first=Ian |date=1991-01-01 |title=Forgotten but not lost: the secret of Coade Stone |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0016787808800727 |journal=Proceedings of the Geologists' Association |language=en |volume=102 |issue=2 |pages=135–138 |doi=10.1016/S0016-7878(08)80072-7 |bibcode=1991PrGA..102..135F |issn=0016-7878|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Geologist James R. Underwood has proposed anthropic rock as a fourth class of rocks alongside igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Underwood |first=James R. |date=2001-02-01 |title=Anthropic rocks as a fourth basic class |url=https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/aeg/eeg/article/7/1/104/60602/Anthropic-rocks-as-a-fourth-basic-class |journal=Environmental and Engineering Geoscience |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=104–110 |doi=10.2113/gseegeosci.7.1.104 |bibcode=2001EEGeo...7..104U |issn=1078-7275|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Building===
{{See also|Building material#Stone or rock|Masonry}}
[[File:Pirunvuoren kivilinna.jpg|thumb|A stonehouse on the hill in [[Sastamala]], Finland]]
[[File:Hochbeet aus Naturstein.jpg|thumb|right|[[Raised-bed gardening|Raised garden bed]] with natural stones]]
Rock varies greatly in strength, from [[quartzites]] having a [[tensile strength]] in excess of 300 [[MPa]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Amadei |first1=B. |title=Strength properties of rocks and rock masses |url=https://ceae.colorado.edu/~amadei/CVEN5768/PDF/NOTES8.pdf |website=Civil, Environmental, and Architectural Engineering |publisher=University of Colorado Boulder |access-date=18 April 2021}}</ref> to sedimentary rock so soft it can be crumbled with bare fingers (that is, it is ''[[friable]]'').<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Jackson |editor1-first=Julia A. |title=Glossary of geology. |date=1997 |publisher=American Geological Institute |location=Alexandria, Virginia |isbn=0922152349 |edition=Fourth |chapter=Friable}}</ref> (For comparison, [[structural steel]] has a tensile strength of around 350 MPa.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjorhovde |first1=Reidar |title=Development and use of high performance steel |journal=Journal of Constructional Steel Research |date=2004 |volume=60 |issue=3–5 |pages=393–400 |doi=10.1016/S0143-974X(03)00118-4 |bibcode=2004JCSR...60..393B }}</ref>) Relatively soft, easily worked sedimentary rock was quarried for construction as early as 4000 BCE in Egypt,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klemm |first1=Dietrich D. |last2=Klemm |first2=Rosemarie |title=The building stones of ancient Egypt – a gift of its geology |journal=Journal of African Earth Sciences |date=2001 |volume=33 |issue=3–4 |pages=631–642 |doi=10.1016/S0899-5362(01)00085-9|bibcode=2001JAfES..33..631K }}</ref> and stone was used to build fortifications in [[Inner Mongolia]] as early as 2800 BCE.<ref>{{cite journal |author1-link=Gideon Shelach-Lavi |last1=Shelach |first1=Gideon |last2=Raphael |first2=Kate |last3=Jaffe |first3=Yitzhak |title=Sanzuodian: the structure, function and social significance of the earliest stone fortified sites in China |journal=Antiquity |date=2011 |volume=85 |issue=327 |pages=11–26 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00067405|s2cid=163488276 }}</ref> The soft rock, [[tuff]], is common in Italy, and the [[Ancient Rome|Romans]] used it for many buildings and bridges.<ref name="jackson-etal-2005">{{cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=M. D. |last2=Marra |first2=F. |last3=Hay |first3=R. L. |last4=Cawood |first4=C. |last5=Winkler |first5=E. M. |title=The Judicious Selection and Preservation of Tuff and Travertine Building Stone in Ancient Rome* |journal=Archaeometry |date=2005 |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=485–510 |doi=10.1111/j.1475-4754.2005.00215.x|doi-access=free |bibcode=2005Archa..47..485J }}</ref> [[Limestone]] was widely used in construction in the Middle Ages in Europe <ref name=ashurst>{{cite book|last1=Ashurst|first1=John|last2=Dimes|first2=Francis G.|title=Conservation of building and decorative stone|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xPFx6bEPspgC&pg=PA117|year=1998|publisher=Butterworth-Heinemann|isbn=978-0-7506-3898-2|page=117}}</ref> and remained popular into the 20th century.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.citylifeontario.com/kingston/ |title= Welcome to the Limestone City |access-date=13 February 2008 |url-status= live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080220171909/http://www.citylifeontario.com/kingston/ |archive-date= 20 February 2008 }}</ref>

===Mining===
{{Main|Mining}}
[[File:UraniumMineUtah.JPG|thumb|left|[[Charles Steen#Mi Vida|Mi Vida uranium mine]] near [[Moab, Utah]]]]
Mining is the extraction of [[value (economics)|valuable]] [[mineral]]s or other [[geology|geological]] materials from the earth, from an [[ore]] body, [[vein (geology)|vein]] or [[Seam (geology)|seam]].<ref>{{cite news |first1=Shekhar |last1=Gajul |title=Underground Mining Equipment Market 2017 Global Key Players, Share, Challenges, Industry Size, Growth Opportunities & Forecast To 2021 |url=https://www.journalistbook.com/2018/07/28/underground-mining-equipment-market-2017-global-key-players-share-challenges-industry-size-growth-opportunities-forecast-to-2021/ |newspaper=Journalist Book |date=28 July 2018 |access-date=28 July 2018 |archive-date=28 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728221613/https://www.journalistbook.com/2018/07/28/underground-mining-equipment-market-2017-global-key-players-share-challenges-industry-size-growth-opportunities-forecast-to-2021/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The term also includes the removal of soil. Materials recovered by mining include [[base metals]], [[precious metals]], [[iron]], [[uranium]], [[coal]], [[diamond]]s, [[limestone]], [[oil shale]], [[Sodium chloride|rock salt]], [[potash]], [[construction aggregate]] and [[dimension stone]]. Mining is required to obtain any material that cannot be grown through [[agriculture|agricultural]] processes, or created [[Chemical synthesis|artificially]] in a [[laboratory]] or [[factory]]. Mining in a wider sense comprises extraction of any [[resource]] (e.g. [[petroleum]], [[natural gas]], [[salt]] or even [[water]]) from the earth.<ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Botin|editor1-first=J.A.|title=Sustainable Management of Mining Operations|date=2009|publisher=Society for Mining, Metallurgy, and Exploration|location=Denver, CO|isbn=978-0-87335-267-3}}</ref>

Mining of rock and metals has been done since [[Prehistory|prehistoric]] times. Modern mining processes involve [[prospecting]] for mineral deposits, analysis of the profit potential of a proposed mine, extraction of the desired materials, and finally reclamation of the land to prepare it for other uses once mining ceases.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Wilson|first1=Arthur|title=The Living Rock: The Story of Metals Since Earliest Times and Their Impact on Developing Civilization|date=1996|publisher=[[Woodhead Publishing]]|location=Cambridge, England|isbn=978-1-85573-301-5}}</ref>

Mining processes may create negative impacts on the environment both during the mining operations and for years after mining has ceased. These potential impacts have led to most of the world's nations adopting regulations to manage negative effects of mining operations.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Terrascope|title=Environmental Risks of Mining |url=http://web.mit.edu/12.000/www/m2016/finalwebsite/problems/mining.html |website=The Future of strategic Natural Resources|publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]|access-date=10 September 2014|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140920190206/http://web.mit.edu/12.000/www/m2016/finalwebsite/problems/mining.html|archive-date=20 September 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

=== Tools ===
{{Main|Stone tool}}
Stone tools have been used for millions of years by humans and earlier [[Hominidae|hominids]]. The Stone Age was a period of widespread stone tool usage.<ref name="nhm.ac.uk">{{Cite web |date=18 August 2010 |title=Oldest tool use and meat-eating revealed &#124; Natural History Museum |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/about-us/news/2010/august/oldest-tool-use-and-meat-eating-revealed75831.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100818123718/http://www.nhm.ac.uk/about-us/news/2010/august/oldest-tool-use-and-meat-eating-revealed75831.html |archive-date=18 August 2010}}</ref> [[Early Stone Age]] tools were simple implements, such as [[hammerstone]]s and sharp flakes. [[Middle Stone Age]] tools featured sharpened points to be used as [[projectile point]]s, awls, or [[Scraper (archaeology)|scrapers]]. [[Late Stone Age]] tools were developed with [[craftsmanship]] and distinct cultural identities.<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 June 2022 |title=Stone Tools |url=https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/behavior/stone-tools |access-date=2022-08-09 |website=The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |language=en}}</ref> Stone tools were largely superseded by copper and bronze tools following the development of [[metallurgy]].
